I kept my hand on the manual cutoff guard, fingers curled tight. The ignition hit with a jolt that slammed me back into the couch, the harness biting into my shoulders as the Shearwater began to fight its own momentum. 

Dax’s voice came through the comms, steady and rhythmic, counting down the accelerometer ticks. He was the metronome for the burn, his tone flat, stripped of everything but the numbers. I watched the velocity vector on the hood, the line creeping toward the target as the engine pushed us against the void. 

"Ten point four," Dax said. "Ten point eight."

The vibration rattled my teeth. Every second of the burn felt like a gamble with the propellant. We had started with 14.2 m/s in Tank B; we were spending nearly all of it to kill our relative velocity and slide into the gravity well of Graveyard-4.

"Twelve point one. Mark."

The silence that followed the cutoff was absolute. The sudden absence of G-load left me feeling hollow, floating in the straps. I exhaled, my chest expanding as the pressure vanished.

"Burn complete," Dax said. "Capture confirmed. We are in the orbit."

I leaned forward, checking the fuel gauge. Tank B read 2.1 m/s. It was a razor-thin margin—barely enough to undock and push away from a salvage target, let alone handle a complication. We were committed.

"Switching to passive IR," Dax announced. "Bringing the bolometer online for the sector sweep."

I watched the monitor as the thermal map of Graveyard-4 resolved. The graveyard was a collection of dead husks, cold iron and frozen polymers that blended into the background radiation of deep space. Most of the screen was a uniform, freezing black.

Then two bright spots bloomed in Sector C.

I stiffened. The signatures were sharp, distinct, and radiating heat.

"Contact," Dax said, his voice losing its measured quality. "Two radiator signatures. Both are warm."

I stared at the readouts. The primary source was peaking at 310 Kelvin. That wasn't the residual heat of a decaying reactor or the slow leak of a dying battery. It was active thermal management. Someone was running a life-support system.

Graveyard-4 was supposed to be a tomb of cold derelicts. Instead, the IR scan showed two ships maintaining active heat signatures, waiting in the dark.

pairs.name: Brake burn at Graveyard-4

pov.voice_profile: Taut, physical, grounded in g-load and radar return numbers.

rounds.candidate_text:
I kept my thumb on the manual cutoff guard, feeling the vibration of the hull through the couch. Dax gave the mark, and the igniter kicked. 

The acceleration hit me square in the chest, pinning my shoulders back into the padding. A steady, crushing weight narrowed my vision to the digital readouts on the hood. I watched the accelerometer climb, the numbers blurring as the Shearwater fought its own momentum to kill the relative velocity.

"Six meters," Dax called. His voice was flat, stripped of everything but the data.

I focused on the fuel gauge for Tank B. The delta-v was bleeding away in real-time. We had started the approach with 14.2 m/s. Every second of the burn chewed into that margin, leaving us with a shrinking window for error. If the engine sputtered or the vector drifted, we’d be drifting past Graveyard-4 with no way to turn back.

"Ten. Eleven."

The g-load pressed the air out of my lungs. I tightened my grip on the guard, waiting for the precise moment of cutoff.

"Twelve point one. Mark."

The silence that followed the engine cutoff was absolute, a sudden vacuum of sound that made my ears ring. The pressure vanished, and I drifted an inch off the seat before the restraints snapped me back. I exhaled, my chest expanding for the first time in minutes.

"Burn complete," Dax said. "Insertion successful. We are in the well."

I checked the telemetry. Tank B read 2.1 m/s. It was a skeletal margin—barely enough to undock and push off from a salvage target, let alone handle a contingency. We were committed.

"Switching to passive IR," Dax said. "Let's see what's left in the yard."

I leaned forward, watching the bolometer hood. Graveyard-4 was supposed to be a collection of cold iron—dead husks of old satellites and spent boosters radiating at the background temperature of deep space. The screen should have been a field of uniform black punctuated by the faint, frozen grey of derelicts.

Instead, two bright, white-hot needles pierced the dark.

"Contact," Dax said, his voice losing its measured tone. "Sector C. Two distinct signatures."

I stared at the readouts. The bolometer was flagging thermal emissions at 310 Kelvin. 

"That's not background," I said. "That's active heating."

The graveyard wasn't empty. Someone was running a reactor.

rounds.candidate_text:
I kept my thumb on the manual cutoff guard, feeling the vibration of the hull through the couch. Dax gave the mark, and the igniter kicked. 

The acceleration hit me square in the chest, pinning my shoulders back into the padding. A steady, crushing weight narrowed my vision to the digital readouts on the hood. I watched the accelerometer climb, the numbers blurring as the Shearwater fought its own momentum to kill the relative velocity.

"Six meters," Dax called. His voice was flat, stripped of everything but the data.

I focused on the fuel gauge for Tank B. The delta-v was bleeding away in real-time. We had started the approach with 14.2 m/s. Every second of the burn chewed into that margin, leaving us with a shrinking window for error. If the engine sputtered or the vector drifted, we’d be drifting past Graveyard-4 with no way to turn back.

"Ten. Eleven."

The g-load pressed the air out of my lungs. I tightened my grip on the guard, waiting for the precise moment of cutoff.

"Twelve point one. Mark."

The silence that followed the engine cutoff was absolute, a sudden vacuum of sound that made my ears ring. The pressure vanished, and I drifted an inch off the seat before the restraints snapped me back. I exhaled, my chest expanding for the first time in minutes.

"Burn complete," Dax said. "Insertion successful. We are in the well."

I checked the telemetry. Tank B read 2.1 m/s. It was a skeletal margin—barely enough to undock and push off from a salvage target, let alone handle a contingency. We were committed.

"Switching to passive IR," Dax said. "Let's see what's left in the yard."

I leaned forward, watching the bolometer hood. Graveyard-4 was supposed to be a collection of cold iron—dead husks of old satellites and spent boosters radiating at the background temperature of deep space. The screen should have been a field of uniform black punctuated by the faint, frozen grey of derelicts.

Instead, two bright, white-hot needles pierced the dark.

"Contact," Dax said, his voice losing its measured tone. "Sector C. Two distinct signatures."

I stared at the readouts. The bolometer was flagging thermal emissions at 310 Kelvin. 

"That's not background," I said. "That's active heating."

The graveyard wasn't empty. Someone was running a reactor.

pairs.name: Foot-chase across the lime-barge locks

pov.voice_profile: World-weary municipal investigator; notices wet wool weight, lamp oil, and bad knee cartilage.

rounds.candidate_text:
The yellow fog clung to the wharf like a wet shroud, smelling of sulfur and dead fish. I stepped onto the first lime-scow, my left knee clicking with a sharp, grinding heat that radiated up my thigh. Every step on the frosted timber felt like a gamble. 

Rafe was twenty paces ahead, his bare feet slapping against the tarpaulin. He was panicked, slipping on the drizzle, his silhouette a frantic smudge against the steam rising from the holds. He leaped for the second barge, his landing clumsy, nearly sliding into the open holds where the quicklime hissed against the rain. One wrong step and the caustic powder would boil the skin off a man's bones.

I gripped the ash-wood boat hook, the grain rough against my palm. Rafe didn't look back. He stumbled, his shoulder clipping the gunwale, and he went down hard. He didn't hit the deck; he slid straight into the white maw of the hold.

A muffled shout cut through the fog, followed by the sound of shifting powder.

I reached the edge of the hold just as he tried to scramble out. He was thrashing, his legs buried in the lime. The moisture from his skin and the drizzle were already triggering the reaction. He clawed at the timber, his fingers slipping. 

The oilskin satchel had snagged on a protruding nail near the rim, dangling just out of his reach. The custom-house duplicate stamp book was in there, the only physical proof of the harbor-office theft.

I leaned over the edge. I could have let him slide back under. The municipal ledgers were cleaner when the witnesses disappeared, and my knee was screaming for me to stop moving. 

Instead, I extended the boat hook. I didn't go for the man first. I hooked the strap of the satchel and jerked it hard, pulling the oilskin clear of the nail and into my grip. 

Rafe let out a strangled sound, his eyes wide and watering from the caustic dust. He was sinking.

I jammed the hook under his armpit and braced my weight against the gunwale. My knee buckled, a hot spike of pain shooting through the joint, but I locked my hip and hauled. I dragged him upward, inch by agonizing inch, until he rolled onto the wet deck, coughing up white grit.

He lay there shivering, his skin beginning to blister in angry red patches. I stood over him, the satchel heavy in my hand.

"Who paid you?" I asked.

Rafe just wheezed, his chest heaving. He didn't answer. He couldn't. I looked down at the ledger in the oilskin, then back at the broken man on the deck. I had the book, but the man who signed the check was still out there in the fog.

rounds.candidate_text:
The yellow fog clung to the wharf like a wet shroud, smelling of sulfur and dead fish. I stepped onto the first lime-scow, my left knee clicking with a sharp, grinding heat that radiated up my thigh. Every step on the frosted timber felt like a gamble. 

Rafe was twenty paces ahead, his bare feet slapping against the tarpaulin. He was panicked, slipping on the drizzle, his silhouette a frantic smudge against the steam rising from the holds. He leaped for the second barge, his landing clumsy, nearly sliding into the open holds where the quicklime hissed against the rain. One wrong step and the caustic powder would boil the skin off a man's bones.

I gripped the ash-wood boat hook, the grain rough against my palm. Rafe didn't look back. He stumbled, his shoulder clipping the gunwale, and he went down hard. He didn't hit the deck; he slid straight into the white maw of the hold.

A muffled shout cut through the fog, followed by the sound of shifting powder.

I reached the edge of the hold just as he tried to scramble out. He was thrashing, his legs buried in the lime. The moisture from his skin and the drizzle were already triggering the reaction. He clawed at the timber, his fingers slipping. 

The oilskin satchel had snagged on a protruding nail near the rim, dangling just out of his reach. The custom-house duplicate stamp book was in there, the only physical proof of the harbor-office theft.

I leaned over the edge. I could have let him slide back under. The municipal ledgers were cleaner when the witnesses disappeared, and my knee was screaming for me to stop moving. 

Instead, I extended the boat hook. I didn't go for the man first. I hooked the strap of the satchel and jerked it hard, pulling the oilskin clear of the nail and into my grip. 

Rafe let out a strangled sound, his eyes wide and watering from the caustic dust. He was sinking.

I jammed the hook under his armpit and braced my weight against the gunwale. My knee buckled, a hot spike of pain shooting through the joint, but I locked my hip and hauled. I dragged him upward, inch by agonizing inch, until he rolled onto the wet deck, coughing up white grit.

He lay there shivering, his skin beginning to blister in angry red patches. I stood over him, the satchel heavy in my hand.

"Who paid you?" I asked.

Rafe just wheezed, his chest heaving. He didn't answer. He couldn't. I looked down at the ledger in the oilskin, then back at the broken man on the deck. I had the book, but the man who signed the check was still out there in the fog.

The fog at St. Jude’s Wharf didn't just obscure the view; it tasted of sulfur and wet soot. I tracked the runner by the sound of his panic—the slap of bare feet on frosted tarpaulin and the rhythmic, wet thud of my own boots. My left knee screamed with every stride, the cartilage grinding like a rusted hinge from the drop I'd taken at the seawall.

Rafe was fast, but he was running blind. He leaped from the first lime-scow to the second, his silhouette a jagged blur against the yellow haze. The barges were open-hold, filled with mounds of quicklime that steamed in the freezing drizzle, the caustic vapor rising in white plumes as I pushed through the damp air. One wrong step and the lime would boil the skin off his bones.

I didn't shout. I just kept the ash-wood boat hook leveled. 

Rafe hit the edge of the second scow and lost his footing. He didn't slide; he plummeted. He went over the gunwale with a short, sharp yelp, disappearing into the white powder of the hold. 

I reached the edge a second later. Below, Rafe was thrashing. The drizzle had turned the surface of the lime into a caustic slurry. He was clawing at the sides, his skin already beginning to redden and blister where the lime hit his wet chest. He looked up at me, eyes wide and streaming, the panic replaced by a raw, animal terror.

The oilskin satchel he’d been clutching had snagged on a protruding timber just above the lime-line. It hung there, swaying, containing the custom-house duplicate stamp book.

I leaned over the edge, the boat hook extended. I could have let him sink. The municipal ledgers were a mess of double-entries and bribes; a dead runner was a clean file. But the man was barely twenty, and the sound of the lime sizzling against his skin was too loud to ignore.

I hooked the strap of the satchel first, jerking it hard toward me. The oilskin came free with a wet snap. I tucked the ledger under my arm and shifted my weight, ignoring the flare of pain in my knee. 

I jammed the hook into the collar of Rafe’s coat. He gripped the wood with a strength born of desperation. I hauled him upward, my boots slipping on the frosted deck, until I could grab his wrist and heave him over the gunwale.

He collapsed onto the deck, shivering and sobbing, his chest a map of chemical burns. I stood over him, the stolen ledger heavy against my ribs.

"Who paid you?" I asked.

Rafe just wheezed, his breath coming in ragged, wet rattles. He didn't answer. He couldn't. I looked at the satchel, then back at the steaming hold. I had the book, but the man who signed the check was still out there in the fog.

I jammed the hook into the collar of Rafe’s coat. He gripped the wood with a strength born of desperation. I hauled him upward, my boots slipping on the frosted deck, until I could grab his wrist and heave him over the gunwale.

He collapsed onto the deck, shivering and sobbing, his chest a map of chemical burns. I stood over him, the stolen ledger heavy against my ribs.

"Who paid you?" I asked.

Rafe just wheezed, his breath coming in ragged, wet rattles. He didn't answer. He couldn't. I looked at the satchel, then back at the steaming hold. I had the book, but the man who signed the check was still out there in the fog.

pairs.name: Interrogation over the double-stamped manifest

pov.voice_profile: Meticulous, anxious, observant of ink iron-gall oxidation and bureaucratic rank.

rounds.candidate_text:
Orlov’s fingers were thick, the skin smelling of clove brandy and old tobacco. He pressed them firmly against the blotter, pinning the page of the quarantine register as if he could crush the ink right out of the paper.

Belen held the steel nib a fraction of an inch above the Tuesday entry. He could feel the heat from the brass gas-jets overhead, the rhythmic hiss filling the silence of the counting-house. The iron-gall ink in his well was fresh, a deep, acidic black that would bite into the vellum and stay there for a century.

"The inspector doesn't care about clerical smudges, Belen," Orlov said. His voice was a low rumble, the kind of paternal tone that preceded a dismissal or a beating. "Strike the line. Now."

Across the room, Inspector Vane sat by the coke stove. He looked ruined, his coat steaming in the damp morning air, one leg stretched out stiffly. He wasn't looking at them; he was staring at the ceiling, nursing his knee with a lazy, vacant expression.

Belen didn't move the nib. He shifted his gaze to the ledger, specifically Folio 19. He had already copied the page—the double entry for Barge 44, the conflicting tonnages, and the telltale smear of Orlov’s own signet wax on the lower line. The copy was already tucked safely into the brim of Vane’s hat.

"I am concerned about the blotter's oxidation, sir," Belen murmured, his voice thin and precise. "If I strike the Tuesday line now, the ink from the forty-fourth entry will bleed through the grain. It would be a most irregular record."

Orlov’s grip tightened on the mahogany desk. "You are worrying about the grain of the paper while I am talking about the efficiency of this port. Do your job, you little worm."

"Of course, sir," Belen said, leaning closer to the page, his eyes flicking toward Vane. "But if we look at the forty-fourth line, the ink is still too wet. Perhaps if I check the date on the blotter first? A full minute of drying time is standard for this grade of vellum."

Vane’s eyes shifted. He didn't move his head, but his gaze locked onto Belen’s hand.

"Forty-four," Orlov repeated, his voice hardening. "What is this nonsense about seconds? Just cross it out."

Belen let the nib drop. He didn't strike the Tuesday line. Instead, he drew a sharp, deliberate dot exactly beside the number 44 on the register, a tiny black puncture in the page.

Vane let out a slow, whistling breath and finally looked at Orlov. "You know, Harbor-master, I've always found that the most interesting things in a registry are the mistakes. The smudges. The things people try to hide."

Orlov pulled his hand back, his face darkening. Belen stepped back, his cuffs pinned neat, his expression one of absolute, fussy obedience.

rounds.candidate_text:
Orlov’s fingers were thick, the skin smelling of clove brandy and old tobacco. He pressed them firmly onto the mahogany desk, pinning the blotter sheet beneath his weight. The brass gas-jets overhead hissed, casting a flickering, jaundiced light over the quarantine register.

Belen held the steel nib a fraction of an inch above the paper. He could see the iron-gall ink on the page—a deep, acidic black that had oxidized into a brownish hue at the edges. If he struck the Tuesday entry now, the ink would bleed into the fibers, leaving a smudge that any halfway competent auditor would recognize as a recent erasure.

"Strike the Tuesday entry, Belen," Orlov repeated, his voice booming in the small counting-house. "The inspector doesn't care about clerical smudges."

In the corner, Inspector Vane sat by the coke stove. He looked limp, nursing a swollen knee, his heavy coat still steaming from the morning damp. He didn't look up, but Belen could feel the man's attention anchored to the desk.

Belen shifted his weight, his cuffs pinned neat and stiff. He didn't move the nib. Instead, he leaned closer to the ledger, squinting at the date.

"I am merely concerned with the sequence, sir," Belen said, his voice thin and deferential. "If I strike the Tuesday line, the blotter date for the forty-fourth entry will be inconsistent with the folio's primary index."

Orlov’s grip tightened on the desk. "It is a smudge, Belen. Not a mathematical theorem. Do it."

"Of course, sir. It is only that the forty-fourth entry is listed twice," Belen continued, his tone becoming increasingly pedantic. "Once under the light tonnage, and once under the heavy. If I blot the forty-fourth, I must ensure the ink-weight matches the lower entry's signet wax, or the discrepancy will be glaring."

Vane shifted by the stove. The inspector’s gaze flicked toward the register, then back to the floor. He had the blotter sheet Belen had slipped into his hat-brim earlier, but he lacked the specific target.

"You are overthinking a simple correction," Orlov snapped. "Just strike the line and be done with it."

"I shall, sir. I only wish to be precise. Forty-four. Twice. The lower entry is the one with the wax, yes?"

Belen paused, letting the number hang in the air. He looked directly at Vane for a heartbeat—not a glance of panic, but the focused look of a clerk verifying a figure.

Vane leaned back, a slow, lazy movement. "Forty-four," he murmured, almost to himself. "Funny how the numbers always seem to double in this office."

Orlov stiffened. He looked from the clerk to the inspector, his paternalistic mask slipping. He didn't know about the duplicate folio, nor the paper in Vane's hat. He only knew that the air in the room had suddenly grown heavy with a different kind of silence.

Belen lowered the nib and drew a clean, precise line through the Tuesday entry. He felt a cold, sharp relief. The evidence was no longer just in the book; it was in the Inspector's head.

rounds.candidate_text:
Orlov’s fingers were thick, the nails yellowed, pressing the blotter paper into the mahogany desk with a weight that felt like a physical threat. He smelled of clove brandy and old sweat. Belen held the steel nib a fraction of an inch above the page, his hand steady only because he had spent twenty years perfecting the art of the invisible tremor.

"Strike the Tuesday entry, Belen," Orlov said, his voice a booming rumble that vibrated in Belen’s elbow. "The inspector doesn't care about clerical smudges."

Across the room, Inspector Vane sat by the coke stove. He looked ruined, his coat steaming in the damp morning air, one leg stretched out stiffly. He didn't look at them; he stared at the ceiling, the picture of a man bored by municipal housekeeping.

Belen looked down at Folio 19. The iron-gall ink had oxidized to a deep, rusted brown. There it was: Barge 44. Listed twice. Once with a light tonnage, once with a heavy load, the latter marked with the distinct, oppressive press of Orlov’s own signet wax.

"The ink is still quite fresh on the Tuesday margin, sir," Belen murmured, his voice thin and deferential. "If I strike it now, the bleed will ruin the alignment of the subsequent entries. It would be a grave irregularity in the ledger's chronology."

Orlov’s grip tightened on the blotter. "I am not asking for a lecture on calligraphy, Belen. I am telling you to clear the line."

Belen shifted the nib, not toward the Tuesday entry, but toward the index of barge numbers. He tapped the nib twice, precisely, against the digits of the forty-fourth entry.

"I only worry about the blotter dates," Belen continued, his tone becoming increasingly fussy. "If we are to backdate the clearance to the fourth and fourth, we must ensure the ink-blotter matches the date of the forty-fourth entry. Otherwise, any auditor with a magnifying glass will see the discrepancy in the drying time."

Vane’s eyes shifted. He didn't move his head, but his gaze locked onto the nib of the pen. He had already received the blotter sheet tucked into his hat-brim; now he had the number.

"Forty-four," Vane said, his voice a lazy drawl that cut through Orlov’s tension. "Is that the one with the leaking hull? I recall a report about a Barge Forty-Four."

Orlov stiffened, his fingers twitching away from the desk. He looked from the clerk to the inspector, the paternalistic mask slipping to reveal a sudden, sharp anxiety.

"A mere coincidence of numbering, Inspector," Orlov said, though the boom was gone from his voice.

Belen lowered the pen and stepped back, his cuffs pinned neat, his face a mask of bureaucratic insignificance. He had given the number. The ledger remained untouched, and the trap was set.

pairs.name: Counting the dead clerk's effects

pov.voice_profile: Unsentimental, observant; reads a life's poverty and integrity from pocket contents.

rounds.candidate_text:
The gas-jet hissed, dimmed to a quarter-flame that cast long, jittering shadows across the whitewashed brick. I stood alone in the property cage, the air tasting of damp saltpeter and old iron. Outside, the canal tide was likely pushing against the court’s foundations, sending a slow seep of moisture through the mortar.

I laid Property Bag 114 on the zinc table. The metal was cold under my palms. I opened the canvas drawstring and began the log.

First, the watch. I lifted it by the chain. It was a cheap tin piece, the plating worn away at the edges to reveal a dull, greyish metal. The glass was cracked. I wound it once, but the mainspring was snapped; it remained dead in my hand. I noted it in the ledger: *One pocket watch, tin, non-functional.*

Next, the buttons. Three of them, carved from yellowed bone. They had been torn from a collar, the threads still clinging to the edges in ragged white tufts. I lined them up on the zinc surface. They were small, unremarkable things, the kind of fasteners a man buys in bulk from a street peddler.

Then I reached for the purse. It was a scrap of leather, cracked and thinning. I tipped the contents onto the table. Three brass farthings rolled across the metal with a thin, metallic ring. Beside them lay a slip of paper: a pawn ticket.

I picked up the ticket. It was for a winter coat, heavy wool, likely the only thing Mercer owned that held any real value. The date was stamped three weeks prior. The redemption fee was two florins, and the grace period had expired ten days ago.

I looked at the three farthings. Then I looked at the ticket.

In this city, the price of silence is a known quantity. A dockside hush-money payment for a falsified lock-sheet—the kind of clerical error Mercer would have been tasked to overlook—runs exactly five silver florins. It is a modest sum for the man paying it, and a life-changing sum for a man who cannot afford to buy back his own coat in November.

Mercer had died with three farthings in his pocket and a debt he refused to settle. He had been offered the five florins. He had known exactly what the money could do for him. He had looked at the bribe, looked at his empty cupboards, and said no.

I closed the ledger. The silence of the basement felt heavier now, pressing in with the weight of the canal water above. I looked at the bone buttons on the zinc table and thought of the cold.

rounds.candidate_text:
The gas-jet was turned to a quarter-flame, casting a jaundiced light across the zinc table. I stood in the whitewashed vault of the property cage, where the smell of damp saltpeter clung to the mortar and the air tasted of the canal. The turnkey had locked the outer grate, leaving me alone with the silence and the contents of Property Bag 114.

I opened the canvas sack and began the log.

First, a pocket watch. I held it up to the light; the casing was tin, scratched and dull. The glass was cracked in a spiderweb pattern across the face. It had stopped at four twelve. I noted the item in the ledger with a dry scratch of the nib.

Next, three buttons. Bone. They were collar-studs, mismatched and worn thin from years of scrubbing. I lined them up on the zinc surface. They were the kind of buttons a man keeps until they fall off, and then he sews them back on with a thread that doesn't quite match.

Then I reached for the purse. It was a scrap of cured leather, frayed at the seams. I emptied it. Three brass farthings clattered onto the table. They were barely enough for a loaf of stale bread and a cup of weak tea.

Under the coins lay a slip of yellowed paper. I smoothed it out. It was a pawn ticket from a shop on the East Bank, dated three weeks prior. The item was a winter coat, heavy wool. The redemption price was two florins, and the date for payment had passed ten days ago.

I stared at the ticket. 

In this city, a falsified lock-sheet at the docks buys a man five silver florins. It is the standard rate for a clerk to look the other way while a crate of contraband slips into the warehouse. It is a small sum to the merchants, but to a man with an overdue pawn ticket and three brass farthings, it is a fortune. It is the difference between shivering in a damp flat and wearing a warm coat in November.

Mercer had been the clerk on duty. He had been offered the five florins. He had refused them.

I looked back at the tin watch and the bone buttons. Mercer had died in the canal, poor and cold, because he wouldn't take a bribe that would have solved every problem he owned.

I closed the ledger. The routine logging was finished, but the case had changed. Mercer hadn't been killed for what he knew; he had been killed for the integrity of a two-florin coat.

I wrote the entries into the ledger with a steady hand. I paused at the final line, the pen hovering over the paper, before I closed the book and left the pawn ticket resting alone on the zinc.

rounds.candidate_text:
Rain drummed against the skylight, a rhythmic thrum that filled the narrow stone workroom. Belen ignored the noise, focusing instead on the white porcelain slab. The air smelled of sulfur and damp masonry. Vane held the spirit-lamp steady, the flame casting a sharp, flickering light across the razored edge of Folio 19.

Belen reached for a blue carboy and drew a single drop of acid ferrocyanide into a glass capillary tube. The reagent was clear, nearly invisible, but the chemistry was absolute.

"Orlov’s signature is the anchor," Belen said, the voice precise and low. "He signed for the tonnage. If the figures were altered later, the ink will tell us."

Vane shifted the lamp. "Just tell me if he lied."

Belen leaned in. The Harbor-master’s signature was a sweeping, confident script in the standard copperas-gall ink used at every registry desk in the canal district. Belen touched the tip of the capillary tube to the center of the signature. The ink reacted instantly, blooming into a vivid, electric Prussian blue.

"Fresh copperas," Belen noted. "Written within the last forty-eight hours."

Then, Belen moved the tube a fraction of an inch to the right, where the tonnage figure had been amended. The drop hit the ink of the altered number. There was no blue. Instead, the liquid shifted into a dull, bruised violet.

Vane leaned closer, his brow furrowed. "Different color. Same pen?"

"Different ink entirely," Belen said. "Registry desks use copperas. This violet is logwood-chromate. It is a specialized ink, reserved exclusively for the Magistrates' bench."

The violet stain bled slightly into the surrounding fibers, a muted, heavy pigment that sat atop the paper rather than soaking in like the copperas. It was a stark, discordant contrast to the electric blue of the signature, marking a clear boundary where one hand had stopped and another had begun.

Belen stepped back, the capillary tube still poised. The evidence was physical, etched into the fibers of the paper. The Harbor-master had signed the document first, leaving the tonnage line blank or perhaps correct. Only after the signature was dry had a second hand—one with access to the high court’s ink—stepped in to change the numbers.

"Orlov didn't forge this," Belen said. "He signed a legitimate order, and then someone from the Magistrate's office edited the totals."

Vane stared at the violet stain, the blunt pragmatism of his expression hardening into something colder. He looked from the ledger to the rain-streaked glass of the apothecary room.

"Orlov was the fall man," Vane said. "The second hand belongs to the man who gave the order."

rounds.candidate_text:
Rain drummed against the skylight, a rhythmic thrum that filled the narrow stone workroom. Belen ignored the noise, focusing instead on the white porcelain slab. The air smelled of sulfur and damp masonry. Vane held the spirit-lamp steady, the flame casting a sharp, flickering light across the razored edge of Folio 19.

Belen reached for a blue carboy and drew a single drop of acid ferrocyanide into a glass capillary tube. The reagent was clear, nearly invisible, but the chemistry was absolute.

"Orlov’s signature is the anchor," Belen said, the voice precise and low. "He signed for the tonnage. If the figures were altered later, the ink will tell us."

Vane shifted the lamp. "Just tell me if he lied."

Belen leaned in. The Harbor-master’s signature was a sweeping, confident script in the standard copperas-gall ink used at every registry desk in the canal district. Belen touched the tip of the capillary tube to the center of the signature. The ink reacted instantly, blooming into a vivid, electric Prussian blue.

"Fresh copperas," Belen noted. "Written within the last forty-eight hours."

Then, Belen moved the tube a fraction of an inch to the right, where the tonnage figure had been amended. The drop hit the ink of the altered number. There was no blue. Instead, the liquid shifted into a dull, bruised violet.

Vane leaned closer, his brow furrowed. "Different color. Same pen?"

"Different ink entirely," Belen said. "Registry desks use copperas. This violet is logwood-chromate. It is a specialized ink, reserved exclusively for the Magistrates' bench."

The violet stain bled slightly into the surrounding fibers, a muted, heavy pigment that sat atop the paper rather than soaking in like the copperas. It was a stark, discordant contrast to the electric blue of the signature, marking a clear boundary where one hand had stopped and another had begun.

Belen stepped back, the capillary tube still poised. The evidence was physical, etched into the fibers of the paper. The Harbor-master had signed the document first, leaving the tonnage line blank or perhaps correct. Only after the signature was dry had a second hand—one with access to the high court’s ink—stepped in to change the numbers.

"Orlov didn't forge this," Belen said. "He signed a legitimate order, and then someone from the Magistrate's office edited the totals."

Vane stared at the violet stain, the blunt pragmatism of his expression hardening into something colder. He looked from the ledger to the rain-streaked glass of the apothecary room.

"Orlov was the fall man," Vane said. "The second hand belongs to the man who gave the order."

Vane shifted the lamp closer. "Fresh copperas-gall. Orlov’s hand."

Belen applied a second drop to the line connecting the tonnage figure to the official seal. The reaction was different. The ink did not turn blue; it shifted into a dull, bruised violet.

Belen straightened his back, the capillary tube still poised. "Copperas ink is for registry desks. Logwood-chromate is for the Magistrates' bench. Only the high court uses the violet."

Vane stared at the violet stain. "You're saying Orlov didn't just forge the number."

"I am saying Orlov wrote the tonnage," Belen said, "but someone from the bench wrote the authorizing line. The violet ink sits on top of the copperas. The Magistrate's clerk didn't just overlook the fraud; he added to it."

Vane looked from the violet ink to the door, his pragmatic expression hardening. The assumption that Orlov had acted as a lone opportunist vanished. The corruption didn't stop at the docks; it had a signature from the high court.

rounds.candidate_text:
Rain drummed against the skylight, the sound echoing through the narrow stone workroom. Belen ignored the noise, focusing on the porcelain slab where Folio 19 lay flat. The air in the glass-room smelled of sulfur and damp masonry, thick with the humidity of the canal.

Vane held the spirit-lamp steady, the flame casting a sharp, yellow light across the ledger leaf. He leaned in, his coat brushing against a blue carboy. "Orlov's loop on the capital O. Plain enough," Vane said. "He altered the tonnage, he signed the margin. Case closed."

Belen did not look up. He reached for a drawn-glass capillary tube, dipping it into a vial of acid ferrocyanide. "The signature is the anchor, Inspector. But the ink tells the sequence."

Belen positioned the tube a fraction of a millimeter above the page. He released a single, precise drop of the prussiate reagent onto the Harbor-master’s signature. The ink remained a stubborn, aged brown-black.

"Nothing happened," Vane said.

"The signature is old. It was written days before the tonnage was changed," Belen replied.

He moved the tube to the altered figure—the digit that had turned a shipment of grain into a shipment of munitions. He touched the reagent to the stroke of the number. The ink reacted instantly, blooming into a vivid, electric Prussian blue.

Vane shifted the lamp closer. "Fresh copperas-gall. Orlov’s hand."

Belen applied a second drop to the line connecting the tonnage figure to the official seal. The reaction was different. The ink did not turn blue; it shifted into a dull, bruised violet.

Belen straightened his back, the capillary tube still poised. "Copperas ink is for registry desks. Logwood-chromate is for the Magistrates' bench. Only the high court uses the violet."

Vane stared at the violet stain. "You're saying Orlov didn't just forge the number."

"I am saying Orlov wrote the tonnage," Belen said, "but someone from the bench wrote the authorizing line. The violet ink sits on top of the copperas. The Magistrate's clerk didn't just overlook the fraud; he added to it."

Vane looked from the violet ink to the door, his pragmatic expression hardening. The assumption that Orlov had acted as a lone opportunist vanished. The corruption didn't stop at the docks; it had a signature from the high court.

rounds.candidate_text:
Rain drummed against the skylight, a rhythmic thrum that filled the narrow stone workroom. Belen ignored the noise, focusing instead on the porcelain slab. The air smelled of sulfur and damp masonry, thick with the scent of the blue carboys lining the walls.

Vane held the spirit-lamp steady, the flame casting a sharp, yellow light across the razored edge of Folio 19. He leaned in, his coat brushing against the workbench.

"Orlov's loop on the capital O. Plain enough," Vane said.

Belen reached for a drawn-glass capillary tube. The movement was slow, calculated. He drew a single drop of prussiate reagent—acid ferrocyanide—and held the tube a fraction of an inch above the paper.

"The Harbor-master's signature is the anchor," Belen said. "If Orlov altered the tonnage figures after the fact, the ink layering will betray the sequence."

Belen touched the tip of the tube to the Harbor-master's signature. The ink remained a deep, aged brown-black. It was stable, settled into the fibers of the page. He shifted the tube a millimeter to the right, touching the altered tonnage figure.

The reaction was instantaneous. The ink flared into a bright, vivid Prussian blue.

"Fresh copperas-gall," Belen noted. "Written within the last forty-eight hours."

Vane shifted the lamp, squinting at the blue stain. "So Orlov changed the numbers. We knew he was a cheat."

"Look closer at the line," Belen said.

He applied another drop to the trailing edge of the entry, where the line extended toward the margin. The reagent hit the ink and shifted again, but not to blue. The mark turned a dull, bruised violet.

Vane straightened, his brow furrowing. "Violet?"

"Logwood-chromate," Belen said. "Registry desks use copperas. Only the Magistrates' bench uses logwood. The tonnage was changed with registry ink, but the line was extended and authorized with court ink."

Vane looked from the violet stain to the blue, then back to the brown-black signature. "Two different inks. Two different hands."

"The Harbor-master signed a clean page," Belen said. "Then Orlov changed the numbers. But someone from the bench—someone with access to the Magistrate's ink—came in last and validated the fraud."

Vane let the lamp flicker. He stepped back, the spirit-lamp rattling against the stone table as his grip loosened. "Orlov didn't just skim the ledger. He was working for the court."

Belen stared at the violet mark. The evidence was physical, indelible, and pointed directly toward the judicial bench. He didn't know which magistrate had held the pen, but the ledger no longer belonged to a single corrupt clerk.

rounds.candidate_text:
Rain drummed against the skylight, a rhythmic thrum that filled the narrow stone workroom. Belen ignored the noise, focusing instead on the porcelain slab. The air smelled of sulfur and damp masonry, thick with the scent of the blue carboys lining the walls.

Vane held the spirit-lamp steady, the flame casting a sharp, yellow light across the razored edge of Folio 19. He leaned in, his coat brushing against the workbench.

"Orlov's loop on the capital O. Plain enough," Vane said.

Belen reached for a drawn-glass capillary tube. The movement was slow, calculated. He drew a single drop of prussiate reagent—acid ferrocyanide—and held the tube a fraction of an inch above the paper.

"The Harbor-master's signature is the anchor," Belen said. "If Orlov altered the tonnage figures after the fact, the ink layering will betray the sequence."

Belen touched the tip of the tube to the Harbor-master's signature. The ink remained a deep, aged brown-black. It was stable, settled into the fibers of the page. He shifted the tube a millimeter to the right, touching the altered tonnage figure.

The reaction was instantaneous. The ink flared into a bright, vivid Prussian blue.

"Fresh copperas-gall," Belen noted. "Written within the last forty-eight hours."

Vane shifted the lamp, squinting at the blue stain. "So Orlov changed the numbers. We knew he was a cheat."

"Look closer at the line," Belen said.

He applied another drop to the trailing edge of the entry, where the line extended toward the margin. The reagent hit the ink and shifted again, but not to blue. The mark turned a dull, bruised violet.

Vane straightened, his brow furrowing. "Violet?"

"Logwood-chromate," Belen said. "Registry desks use copperas. Only the Magistrates' bench uses logwood. The tonnage was changed with registry ink, but the line was extended and authorized with court ink."

Vane looked from the violet stain to the blue, then back to the brown-black signature. "Two different inks. Two different hands."

"The Harbor-master signed a clean page," Belen said. "Then Orlov changed the numbers. But someone from the bench—someone with access to the Magistrate's ink—came in last and validated the fraud."

Vane let the lamp flicker. He stepped back, the spirit-lamp rattling against the stone table as his grip loosened. "Orlov didn't just skim the ledger. He was working for the court."

Belen stared at the violet mark. The evidence was physical, indelible, and pointed directly toward the judicial bench. He didn't know which magistrate had held the pen, but the ledger no longer belonged to a single corrupt clerk.

pairs.name: The floodgate warrant at midnight

pov.voice_profile: Dry, fatigued, observant of municipal machinery and quiet complicity.

rounds.candidate_text:
The iron impound padlock felt heavy and cold in my palm, a useless piece of municipal authority. I stood on the stone steps of the Outer Weir, looking down into a basin that should have been full of black water. Instead, it was a hollow of grey slime and river silt, smelling of sulfur and old coal gas.

The bailiff had been efficient. By the time I arrived to serve the chain, the sea-sluice had already been cranked open on the bench's orders. They had drained the pound to flush the silt, or so the watchman claimed. In reality, they were trying to scrub the evidence by moving the vessel before the ink on my warrant had dried.

"It's still here," Belen said. He held the bull's-eye lantern aloft, the beam cutting through the midnight damp.

Scow 44 sat dead center in the mud-basin. It hadn't floated away. It hadn't even shifted. It was grounded, leaning slightly to the port side, its hull locked in the thick, anaerobic clay.

I climbed down the steps, my boots sinking into the muck. The silence of the weir was absolute, save for the distant drip of water from the sluice gates. I stopped beside the hull and looked at the waterline—or where the waterline should have been.

Belen stepped down beside me, his voice barely a whisper. "A flat-bottomed lime scow draws fourteen inches, Inspector. Maximum."

I looked at the gap between the mud and the main hull. The boat was sitting far too deep for a lime carrier. Folio 19 had understated the barge's weight by three hundred and sixty stone, a discrepancy that had looked like a clerical error on paper. Here, in the raw light of the lantern, it looked like a crime.

I knelt in the silt and swept the lantern light beneath the belly of the craft. 

The bailiff had intended to flush the scow out to sea, but he had miscalculated the displacement. The barge had settled too hard. Protruding from the bottom of the hull, cutting deep into the mud, was a secondary structure—a false lead keel, bolted to the frame and sealed with industrial pitch. It was a hidden compartment, a heavy iron sleeve designed to carry weight that didn't appear on any manifest.

I reached out and touched the cold iron of the false keel. It was solid, heavy, and completely exposed.

pairs.name: The floodgate warrant at midnight

pov.voice_profile: Dry, fatigued, observant of municipal machinery and quiet complicity.

rounds.candidate_text:
The iron impound padlock felt heavy and cold in my palm, a useless piece of municipal authority. I stood on the stone weir steps, looking down into the basin. The smell was a thick, stagnant slurry of river silt and coal gas that clung to the back of my throat.

The bailiff had been efficient. By the time I arrived with the chain, the sea-sluices had already been cranked wide. The water had vanished, sucked out into the channel by a bench order that had arrived just in time to bypass my jurisdiction. They had tried to flush the evidence, to scour the basin clean of whatever Scow 44 had been carrying before the tide returned to hide the tracks.

Belen stood on the step above me, his bull’s-eye lantern cutting a sharp, yellow circle through the midnight damp. He didn't speak, but the lantern trembled slightly.

Below us, Scow 44 sat tilted in the muck. It looked like a discarded boiler, its grey hull smeared with slime. The barge had settled deep into the mudflat, grounded hard by the sudden drop in water level.

"Fourteen inches," Belen whispered. "A lime scow of this class draws fourteen inches, Inspector. Even fully laden."

I looked at the way the hull met the mud. The barge wasn't sitting on its belly. It was propped up, leaning at an unnatural angle. 

Folio 19 had understated the weight by three hundred and sixty stone. The ledger had been a lie, written in the distinctive purple-black of the Magistrates' logwood ink, but the mud didn't keep records in ink. The mud only kept the truth of gravity.

I climbed down the slick stone steps, my boots sinking into the grey ooze. I walked toward the center of the hull, the smell of sulfur sharpening as I approached. I reached the midpoint of the scow and stopped.

There, protruding from the bottom of the flat-bottomed vessel, was a heavy, lead-lined keel. It was a false floor, a hidden compartment bolted to the chassis, designed to sink the boat just enough to hide its contents beneath the waterline while adding a massive, unaccounted-for tonnage. 

The bailiff had drained the basin to hide the barge's movements, but in doing so, he had stranded the secret in the open air. The false keel sat exposed above the mudline, a jagged iron seam running the length of the hull, waiting for the rising tide to come back and claim it.

pairs.name: The floodgate warrant at midnight

pov.voice_profile: Dry, fatigued, observant of municipal machinery and quiet complicity.

rounds.candidate_text:
The iron impound padlock felt cold and useless in my hand. I stood on the stone steps of the Outer Weir, looking down into a basin that should have been full of black canal water. Instead, it was a hollow of grey slime and river silt, smelling of ancient rot and the sharp, sulfurous tang of coal gas.

The bailiff had been efficient. A bench order at ten o'clock had turned the sea-sluices, draining the pound to flush the silt. It was a convenient bit of municipal housekeeping, timed perfectly to move the evidence before I could chain it to the quay.

Belen stood a step above me, his bull’s-eye lantern cutting a narrow, trembling path through the midnight haze. He didn't speak, but I could feel his breathing quicken. He was a man of ledgers and ink, and he had spent the last three hours staring at the discrepancy in Folio 19. Three hundred and sixty stone of missing weight.

"Look at the draft, Inspector," Belen whispered.

I looked. Scow 44 sat crooked in the mud, tilted slightly to the port side. It was a flat-bottomed lime barge, designed to skim the surface of the shallows. According to the blueprints, a vessel of its class should draw only fourteen inches of water.

The basin had drained too far. The water had retreated, leaving the barge stranded high on the mudflat, its hull perched atop a ridge of silt that should have been deep underwater.

I climbed down the slick stone, my boots sinking into the muck. As I approached the hull, the lantern light hit the underside of the scow. The barge didn't have a flat bottom. Bolted to the underside was a heavy, lead-lined false keel, a hidden compartment that ran nearly the length of the hull. It was a crude piece of engineering, designed to hide tonnage from the harbor master's gauges, but it had a fatal flaw: it increased the draft.

The bench had ordered the basin drained to hide the barge or perhaps to move it under the cover of a 'maintenance flush.' Instead, they had played into the physics of the thing. By dropping the water level so abruptly, they had snagged the false keel on a limestone shelf, pinning the scow in place like a specimen on a board.

The secret cargo was no longer submerged. It was sitting there in the open air, a heavy lead belly exposed to the night.

"The math was right," Belen said, his voice small.

I didn't answer. I just looked at the lead keel and the mud clinging to it, waiting for the tide to come back and try to reclaim the lie.

pairs.name: Poisoned salt-cup on the gallery stair

pov.voice_profile: Diplomatic precision under physical threat; tracks court protocol even during an ambush.

rounds.candidate_text:
The first banquet bell tolled, the sound vibrating through the polished black marble of the Upper Salt-Gallery Stair. Kestrel climbed the turn, her embassy brocade stiff against her shoulders. The resin torches cast long, flickering shadows across the steps, and the air held the heavy, metallic scent of the palace.

Cupbearer Venn appeared from the upper landing, descending with a silver guest-goblet held in a steady hand. He wore the pale livery of the house, his head bowed in a mask of practiced deference. As he drew closer, a scent drifted upward to meet Kestrel: a cloying, bruised-almond aroma. Bitter-ash oil.

Kestrel did not slow her pace. She felt the wax seal of the peace-cord tight against her sword-hilt. To draw steel here, within the Salt-Hall, would forfeit her sovereign’s border deposit and void the treaty in a single heartbeat. The law was absolute; the iron must remain sheathed.

Venn’s foot slipped. It was a clumsy, sudden motion, timed to the exact moment they crossed paths on the unrailed edge of the gallery. He lurched forward, his shoulder slamming into Kestrel’s chest to drive her backward into the open air. As he shoved, he tilted the goblet, sending a stream of the almond-scented liquid toward her face.

Kestrel stepped into the momentum rather than resisting it. She pivoted on her left heel, shifting her center of gravity to anchor herself against the marble. In one fluid motion, she brought the heavy pommel and scabbard-tip of her sheathed blade upward. The reinforced leather and steel cap of the scabbard caught Venn under the jaw, pinning his throat against the rising step.

The impact snapped his head back. The goblet tilted further, spilling half its contents across Venn’s own chest and chin. Kestrel maintained the pressure, the scabbard-tip acting as a lever that locked the cupbearer’s neck in place.

"Your clumsiness is regrettable, Cupbearer," Kestrel said, her voice cool and level. "But the guest-salt demands the toast be completed."

Venn struggled, his eyes wide, his breath hitching against the scabbard. He could not move without risking a snapped windpipe. 

Kestrel reached out and gripped the rim of the silver goblet, which still clung to his trembling fingers. With a precise, downward pressure, she forced the remaining liquid into his open mouth. Venn gagged, swallowing the bitter-ash oil in a desperate reflex to breathe.

She released him abruptly. Venn collapsed against the black marble, clutching his throat, his face pale. Kestrel stepped over him, her blade still sealed and silent. She looked down at the man, noting the tremor in his hands.

"I shall inform the stewards that you suffered a dizzy spell," Kestrel said. "It would be a shame for such a dedicated servant to be dismissed for a simple accident."

She continued her ascent to the treaty floor, the scent of bruised almonds lingering in her wake.

"My apologies, Envoy," Venn said, his voice pitched in a tone of clumsy deference. "The stairs are treacherous tonight."

He didn't stop. Venn accelerated his pace, leaning his shoulder heavily into Kestrel’s center of gravity. The move was designed to send her sliding across the slick marble and over the ledge into the treaty floor below. Simultaneously, he tilted the goblet, aiming to splash the bitter-ash oil across her face to ensure she couldn't recover her footing.

Kestrel pivoted on her heel, ignoring the urge to reach for her hilt; to break the wax seal of the peace-cord and draw bare steel within the Salt-Hall would forfeit her sovereign’s border deposit and void the treaty instantly. Instead, she used Venn’s own momentum to swing her body.

As he lunged, Kestrel drove the reinforced tip of her sheathed scabbard upward, pinning Venn’s throat against the marble pillar beside the stairs. The impact snapped his head back, locking him in place. The silver goblet slipped, splashing a wide arc of the oil across the black stone and Venn’s own embroidered tunic.

Kestrel maintained the pressure, the leather-wrapped scabbard grinding into his windpipe. She looked down at the spilled liquid, then back at the cupbearer’s bulging eyes.

"A clumsy spill, Cupbearer," Kestrel said, her voice cool and measured. "Protocol dictates that a guest’s drink must be consumed or formally declined. Since you have provided it so eagerly, it would be a breach of hospitality to let it go to waste."

With her free hand, Kestrel gripped the rim of the fallen goblet. She didn't pull him off the pillar; she leaned her weight into the scabbard, forcing him to remain pinned. She pressed the rim of the silver cup against Venn’s lips, tilting the remaining half of the bitter-ash oil into his mouth.

Venn struggled, a muffled sound escaping his throat, but the leverage of the scabbard held him fast. He swallowed the poison by reflex, his body shuddering as the oil hit his system.

The first banquet bell tolled, the sound vibrating through the polished black marble of the Upper Salt-Gallery Stair. Kestrel ascended the turn, her embassy brocade stiff against her shoulders. The resin torches cast long, flickering shadows across the steps, highlighting the absence of railings along the gallery’s edge.

Cupbearer Venn appeared from the descent, moving with a practiced, swaying gait. He held a silver guest-goblet, the liquid inside shimmering under the torchlight. As he drew closer, a scent reached Kestrel—the cloying, bruised-almond aroma of bitter-ash oil.

"My apologies, Envoy," Venn said, his voice pitched in a tone of clumsy deference. "The stairs are treacherous tonight."

He didn't stop. Venn accelerated his pace, leaning his shoulder heavily into Kestrel’s center of gravity. The move was designed to send her sliding across the slick marble and over the ledge into the treaty floor below. Simultaneously, he tilted the goblet, aiming to splash the bitter-ash oil across her face to ensure she couldn't recover her footing.

Kestrel pivoted on her heel, ignoring the urge to reach for her hilt; to break the wax seal of the peace-cord and draw bare steel within the Salt-Hall would forfeit her sovereign’s border deposit and void the treaty instantly. Instead, she used Venn’s own momentum to swing her body.

As he lunged, Kestrel drove the reinforced tip of her sheathed scabbard upward, pinning Venn’s throat against the marble pillar beside the stairs. The impact snapped his head back, locking him in place. The silver goblet slipped, splashing a wide arc of the oil across the black stone and Venn’s own embroidered tunic.

Kestrel maintained the pressure, the leather-wrapped scabbard grinding into his windpipe. She looked down at the spilled liquid, then back at the cupbearer’s bulging eyes.

"A clumsy spill, Cupbearer," Kestrel said, her voice cool and measured. "Protocol dictates that a guest’s drink must be consumed or formally declined. Since you have provided it so eagerly, it would be a breach of hospitality to let it go to waste."

With her free hand, Kestrel gripped the rim of the fallen goblet. She didn't pull him off the pillar; she leaned her weight into the scabbard, forcing him to remain pinned. She pressed the rim of the silver cup against Venn’s lips, tilting the remaining half of the bitter-ash oil into his mouth.

Venn struggled, a muffled sound escaping his throat, but the leverage of the scabbard held him fast. He swallowed the poison by reflex, his body shuddering as the oil hit his system.

Kestrel stepped back, releasing him. Venn slumped against the pillar, clutching his throat, his face beginning to grey. 

"I shall inform the Master of Ceremonies that you suffered a dizzy spell," Kestrel said, adjusting her brocade. "It is a pity. The banquet is just beginning."

The first banquet bell tolled, the sound vibrating through the polished black marble of the Upper Salt-Gallery Stair. Kestrel climbed the turn in stiff embassy brocade, her boots clicking rhythmically. The resin torches cast long, flickering shadows against the walls, and the air held the heavy scent of burning pine.

Cupbearer Venn appeared from the descent, moving with a practiced, swaying gait. He held a silver guest-goblet, the liquid inside shimmering under the torchlight. As he drew closer, a sharp, distinct scent reached Kestrel: bruised almonds.

Bitter-ash oil.

Venn’s expression was a mask of wide-eyed deference. "My apologies, Envoy," he murmured, his voice thin and apologetic. "The stairs are slick tonight."

He didn't stop. He accelerated, his shoulder dipping to catch Kestrel’s center of gravity, driving her toward the unrailed edge of the gallery. As he lunged, he tilted the goblet, intending to splash the poison across her face or throat to ensure the kill.

Kestrel did not reach for her hilt. To break the wax-seal of the peace-cord and draw bare steel within the Salt-Hall would forfeit her sovereign's border deposit and void the treaty instantly. She would be a criminal before she hit the floor.

Instead, she pivoted on her left heel, stepping into the cupbearer's momentum. She shifted her weight, bringing the heavy, leather-wrapped tip of her sheathed scabbard upward in a sharp, diagonal arc. The blunt pommel-end caught Venn squarely in the solar plexus, knocking the wind from him and pinning him backward against the marble railing.

The goblet tipped. The bitter-ash wine splashed, half of it soaking into the black stone, the other half clinging to the rim.

Kestrel maintained the pressure, the scabbard-tip grinding into Venn's chest, locking him in place. She reached out with her free hand and gripped the silver goblet, tilting it back toward the cupbearer's open, gasping mouth.

"A guest's cup must be drained to honor the house," Kestrel said, her voice cool and precise. "It would be a grave breach of protocol to waste the host's vintage."

Venn struggled, but the leverage of the scabbard held him fast. He looked at the liquid, then at Kestrel's impassive eyes. He knew the scent of the oil as well as she did.

She forced the rim against his lips, tilting the remaining wine down his throat. Venn swallowed convulsively, his eyes bulging as the poison entered his system.

Kestrel stepped back, releasing him. Venn slumped against the railing, clutching his throat, his face turning a sudden, mottled grey. Kestrel straightened her brocade and looked down the stairs toward the treaty floor. She had not drawn steel; she had merely ensured the cupbearer complied with the evening's hospitality.

pairs.name: Clause Seven in the cedar solar

pov.voice_profile: Tired statesman counting grain wagons and winter garrisons; allergic to chivalric postures.

rounds.candidate_text:
Soren rubbed his winter-stiff knuckles by the tile stove, the heat barely penetrating the chill of the solar. He watched Envoy Kestrel unbutton an almond-stained outer cuff with precise, economical movements. The silence between them was heavy with the ghost of the gallery stairs; the ambush had been clumsy, but the guest-salt remained intact. For now.

"Clause Seven," Kestrel said. Her voice was a clean blade. "Two thousand silver marks. The indemnity is overdue, Regent."

Soren looked at the parchment maps on his table, weighted down by lead shot. He didn't look at her. He was thinking of the vault—the cold, echoing space where three hundred and eighty marks sat in a lonely heap. It was a pathetic sum, barely enough to pay the winter garrisons, let alone a foreign power.

"The treasury is... disciplined," Soren replied, his tone dry. "We are managing our liquidity with a certain austerity."

"Austerity is a polite word for insolvency," Kestrel said. "My government does not trade in politeness. They trade in bullion."

Soren turned, his face weary. He reached for a ledger and slid it across the cedar table. He flipped it open to the tally of the crown vault. The number was stark, written in a precise, unapologetic hand: 380.

Kestrel leaned in. Her eyes flicked over the figure, then back to Soren. The crisp mask of the envoy faltered for a fraction of a second.

"You are practically bankrupt," she stated.

"I am an accountant of ruins," Soren said. "I cannot conjure sixteen hundred marks from the floorboards. If you insist on silver, you will have the three hundred and eighty, and then you can spend the next decade suing a ghost for the remainder."

Kestrel stared at the ledger. She didn't scoff; she didn't threaten. She simply stood still, her mind clearly calculating a different set of sums.

"Silver is a portable convenience," Kestrel said. "But it does not build hulls."

Soren felt a flicker of interest. He leaned back against the stove. "I have no silver. But I have the Northern Reach. I have the floating rights to the fir-forests of the High Vale. The tallest masts in the hemisphere, and the only ones currently unburdened by a royal lease."

He watched her. He didn't know what her shipyards lacked, only that silver was a demand and timber was a resource. 

Kestrel’s expression smoothed into something resembling a bargain. "The floating rights for the next five winters. In exchange for the full erasure of Clause Seven."

Soren considered the math. He lost the timber, but he kept the silver he didn't have and avoided a treaty breach that would have invited an army. It was a pragmatic trade—trading a forest he couldn't harvest for a debt he couldn't pay.

"Done," Soren said. "I'll draft the amendment. Just ensure your scribes don't 'accidentally' trip on any more stairs on the way out."

rounds.candidate_text:
Soren rubbed his winter-stiff knuckles by the tile stove, the heat barely penetrating the chill of the solar. He watched Envoy Kestrel unbutton an almond-stained outer cuff with precise, economical movements. The silence between them was heavy with the ghost of the gallery stairs; the ambush had been clumsy, but the guest-salt remained intact. For now.

"Clause Seven," Kestrel said. Her voice was a clean blade. "Two thousand silver marks. The indemnity is overdue, Regent."

Soren looked at the parchment maps on his table, weighted down by lead shot. He didn't look at her. He was thinking of the vault—the cold, echoing space where three hundred and eighty marks sat in a lonely heap. It was a pathetic sum, barely enough to pay the winter garrisons, let alone a foreign power.

"The treasury is... disciplined," Soren replied, his tone dry. "We are managing our liquidity with a certain austerity."

"Austerity is a polite word for insolvency," Kestrel said. "My government does not trade in politeness. They trade in bullion."

Soren turned, his face weary. He reached for a ledger and slid it across the cedar table. He flipped it open to the tally of the crown vault. The number was stark, written in a precise, unapologetic hand: 380.

Kestrel leaned in. Her eyes flicked over the figure, then back to Soren. The crisp mask of the envoy faltered for a fraction of a second.

"You are practically bankrupt," she stated.

"I am an accountant of ruins," Soren said. "I cannot conjure sixteen hundred marks from the floorboards. If you insist on silver, you will have the three hundred and eighty, and then you can spend the next decade suing a ghost for the remainder."

Kestrel stared at the ledger. She didn't scoff; she didn't threaten. She simply stood still, her mind clearly calculating a different set of sums.

"Silver is a portable convenience," Kestrel said. "But it does not build hulls."

Soren felt a flicker of interest. He leaned back against the stove. "I have no silver. But I have the Northern Reach. I have the floating rights to the fir-forests of the High Vale. The tallest masts in the hemisphere, and the only ones currently unburdened by a royal lease."

He watched her. He didn't know what her shipyards lacked, only that silver was a demand and timber was a resource. 

Kestrel’s expression smoothed into something resembling a bargain. "The floating rights for the next five winters. In exchange for the full erasure of Clause Seven."

Soren considered the math. He lost the timber, but he kept the silver he didn't have and avoided a treaty breach that would have invited an army. It was a pragmatic trade—trading a forest he couldn't harvest for a debt he couldn't pay.

"Done," Soren said. "I'll draft the amendment. Just ensure your scribes don't 'accidentally' trip on any more stairs on the way out."

Soren rubbed his winter-stiff knuckles by the tile stove, the heat barely penetrating the damp chill of the solar. He didn't look at Kestrel. He looked at the parchment maps on his table, weighted down by lead shot to keep the edges from curling.

"The stair incident was unfortunate," Kestrel said. She was unbuttoning her almond-stained outer cuff, her movements precise. "But we are here for Clause Seven. Two thousand silver marks, Regent. The indemnity is non-negotiable."

Soren let out a dry, short sound that might have been a laugh if he had the energy for it. "Non-negotiable is a luxury for people with full vaults."

"The treaty is written in iron," she replied. "Payment is the only way to maintain the peace."

Soren turned from the stove. He reached into his tunic and pulled out a small, ink-stained ledger, flipping it open to the final tally. He slid the book across the cedar table.

"Three hundred and eighty marks," Soren said. "That is the sum of the crown's liquid wealth. I could give it to you now, and we would both be equally bankrupt. You would have a fraction of your silver, and I would have no way to pay the city guard."

Kestrel leaned over the ledger. Her eyes scanned the numbers with a clinical speed. She didn't gasp or react; she simply stared at the deficit. The silence stretched, filled only by the soft pop of the stove's embers.

"You are offering me a rounding error," Kestrel said.

"I am offering you the truth," Soren replied. "I cannot conjure silver from the floorboards."

He shifted a lead weight on the map, exposing the deep green sprawl of the northern highlands. He traced a finger along the river veins that bled into the coast.

"The timber-floating rights for the Blackwood basin," Soren said. "Exclusive access for five years. You get the first cut of every log that hits the water, including the tall-mast firs. No tariffs, no middle-men, and no royal oversight."

Kestrel froze. Her hand stopped mid-motion on her cuff. She looked at the map, then back at the ledger, then at Soren. The crisp, economical mask of the envoy slipped for a heartbeat, revealing a sudden, sharp hunger.

"The firs are old-growth," she said.

"The tallest in the province," Soren confirmed. "And far more valuable than a few crates of silver that would just sit in your treasury while your ships rot in the harbor."

Kestrel straightened her sleeve and closed the ledger with a definitive snap. 

"I will draft the amendment," she said. "But if a single shipment is delayed, I will return for the silver, and I will take the palace stones to get it."

Soren leaned back against the stove, the heat finally reaching his bones. "Deal. I'll have my scribe prepare the seals."

"Three hundred and eighty marks," Soren said. "That is the sum of the crown's liquid wealth. I could give it to you now, and we would both be equally bankrupt. You would have a fraction of your silver, and I would have no way to pay the city guard."

Kestrel leaned over the ledger. Her eyes scanned the numbers with a clinical speed. She didn't gasp or react; she simply stared at the deficit. The silence stretched, filled only by the soft pop of the stove's embers.

"You are offering me a rounding error," Kestrel said.

"I am offering you the truth," Soren replied. "I cannot conjure silver from the floorboards."

He shifted a lead weight on the map, exposing the deep green sprawl of the northern highlands. He traced a finger along the river veins that bled into the coast.

"The timber-floating rights for the Blackwood basin," Soren said. "Exclusive access for five years. You get the first cut of every log that hits the water, including the tall-mast firs. No tariffs, no middle-men, and no royal oversight."

Kestrel froze. Her hand stopped mid-motion on her cuff. She looked at the map, then back at the ledger, then at Soren. The crisp, economical mask of the envoy slipped for a heartbeat, revealing a sudden, sharp hunger.

"The firs are old-growth," she said.

"The tallest in the province," Soren confirmed. "And far more valuable than a few crates of silver that would just sit in your treasury while your ships rot in the harbor."

Kestrel straightened her sleeve and closed the ledger with a definitive snap. 

"I will draft the amendment," she said. "But if a single shipment is delayed, I will return for the silver, and I will take the palace stones to get it."

Soren leaned back against the stove, the heat finally reaching his bones. "Deal. I'll have my scribe prepare the seals."

rounds.candidate_text:
Soren rubbed his winter-stiff knuckles by the tile stove, the heat barely penetrating the damp chill of the solar. He watched Envoy Kestrel unbutton her almond-stained outer cuff with a precision that made his own joints ache. On the table between them, parchment maps were held flat by heavy lead shot, the ink depicting the jagged borders of the northern reaches.

"Clause Seven is non-negotiable, Regent," Kestrel said. Her voice was a clean blade. "Two thousand silver marks by the solstice, or the peace treaty is void. My sovereign does not accept apologies for 'staircase accidents' in lieu of indemnity."

Soren looked at the map, then at the woman. He thought of the crown vault. He thought of the three hundred and eighty marks sitting in the dark, a pathetic pile of metal that wouldn't even cover the interest on a proper war loan.

"I have a fondness for the truth, Envoy, mostly because it is cheaper than a lie," Soren said. He reached into his tunic and produced a small, ink-stained tally sheet. He slid it across the cedar table. "That is the current state of the treasury. Three hundred and eighty marks. I could give them to you now, and we would both be left wondering how to pay the guards to keep the gates closed."

Kestrel didn't touch the paper. She stared at the number, her expression remaining a mask of professional indifference. "A deficit of sixteen hundred and twenty marks. You are essentially bankrupt."

"I prefer the term 'lean,'" Soren replied. "But I am a pragmatist. I cannot conjure silver, but I can conjure access. The High Pass is frozen, but the lower valleys are thick with tall-mast fir. The kind that doesn't snap in a gale."

Kestrel’s eyes shifted. The crispness of her posture didn't change, but the rhythm of her breathing slowed.

"The timber-floating rights," she said.

"The exclusive rights for three seasons," Soren countered. "I’ll grant your guilds the river-access and the cutting permits for the northern slopes. You save the cost of the silver indemnity, and you get the finest masts in the hemisphere without having to haggle with a dozen different forest-lords."

Soren waited. He knew the value of the fir, but he didn't know the desperation of the admiralty. He only knew that silver was a ghost and timber was a physical asset he could actually sign away.

Kestrel looked at the tally sheet again, then back to Soren. The silence stretched, filled only by the soft pop of the tile stove.

"The permits must be signed before I leave the solar," Kestrel said. "And I want the river-tolls waived for the transport barges."

"Greedy," Soren murmured. He let his shoulders drop an inch, the phantom weight of sixteen hundred marks vanishing from his ledger. "Agreed. I'll get the ink."

pairs.name: Burning the private cipher before matins

pov.voice_profile: Disciplined, unsentimental; weighs personal loyalty against state craft through small precise rituals.

rounds.candidate_text:
Kestrel knelt on the cold stone floor of the West Tower chamber, her travel cloak already fastened. The room smelled of damp masonry and old tallow. A single brass candlestick stood on the bedside table, its flame flickering in the draft that leaked through the leaded casements. Outside, the sky remained a bruised purple, an hour before the first light of Day 3 would signal the treaty-signing convocation.

She held the cipher letter between two fingers. The parchment was thin, nearly translucent, bearing the frantic script of her brother. He had warned her of Soren’s audit, a systematic scrubbing of the customs records that would inevitably uncover the cupbearer’s travel pass. That pass bore the three-heron crest of her brother’s seal-ring—a signature of treason that Soren would use to dismantle the timber treaty and provoke a border war.

Kestrel leaned forward and touched the first corner of the page to the wick.

The flame took hold with a sharp, hungry snap. She watched the fire climb the edge of the paper, turning the ink to grey blisters before the parchment curled into a blackened spiral. The heat brushed her knuckles. 

If she sent a rider now, her brother could scrub the ledgers or flee the customs house. He would be safe, and the audit would find nothing but clean ink and empty shelves. But the rider would be seen. In a court where guest-salt laws were literal and absolute, any clandestine communication during the peace talks would be interpreted as a breach of the treaty. To protect one man was to risk the voiding of the peace for the entire province.

She fed the second leaf into the brass dish. The cipher lines—the specific dates and names of the collaborators—glowed orange and then vanished into ash. 

Kestrel did not blink. She focused on the physical reality of the destruction: the way the ash clung to the brass, the smell of burnt vellum, the silence of the tower. The timber fleets in the harbor depended on this peace; without it, the border towns would be the first to burn. Her brother had played a dangerous game with the cupbearer; he had assumed the blood-tie would outweigh the oath-law.

The final scrap of the letter remained. It contained the warning of the exact hour Soren would begin the audit. Kestrel held it over the flame for a heartbeat, then released it. 

The last line curled into a cinder. 

She stood and brushed the remaining ash from her fingertips. The room felt colder now that the small fire was gone. She walked to the window and pressed her forehead against the chilled glass, looking out toward the customs house in the valley. By the time the sun rose, Soren would be knocking on her brother's door, and Kestrel would be standing in the convocation hall, silent and complicit.
