The North Scriptorium smelled of kelp smoke and the sour tang of damp vellum. Outside, the gale hammered the sea-wall, a rhythmic thrum that vibrated through the vaulted stone. Prior Malachi did not look up from his charcoal pan; he kept his attention on the ink-horn, warming the fluid with a slow, circular motion.

Jude laid the crushed brass caliper across the Prior's clean vellum sheet. The metal was sheared, a jagged testament to the force required to jam the bell’s yoke. Jude wrapped his pinched thumb in a strip of linen, his jaw tight.

"The bell is muffled, Prior," Jude said. "But the metal is wrong. It’s too soft. The pour didn't set like pure bronze."

Malachi shifted the ink-horn. "The casting process is fraught with variables, Master Jude. The humidity of the coast, the impurities of the ore. We are blessed that it rings at all."

Agnes stepped toward the lectern, the soaked burial roll unfurling beneath her fingers. The ink had bled, but the numbers remained legible. She looked at the Prior, her voice low and steady.

"The rubric of the garth is absolute, Father. Every soul recovered from the tide must be accounted for, their tallies returned to the earth to ensure a quiet passing."

Malachi finally looked up, his expression a mask of clerical patience. "And so it was done. The Halcyon gave us many dead, and we gave them all a Christian resting."

"Forty sailors washed ashore," Agnes said. "I counted the bodies myself as they were hauled from the shingle. I recorded forty names in the register."

Malachi paused. "The spirit of the law permits a certain latitude in the recording of the nameless, Sister. A clerical oversight in the face of such carnage is a mercy, not a failure."

"The register does not falter," Agnes replied. "But the burial roll does. Thirty-two silver neck-tallies were interred in the garth. Eight are missing."

Jude stepped forward, his voice blunt. "Silver in a bronze pour lowers the melting point. It changes the ring. I felt it in the metal, Prior. You didn't just cast a bell; you cast a hoard."

Malachi’s hand froze over the charcoal. The evasive cadence of his voice sharpened. "The abbey is burdened by the dike-loan. The bailiff’s assay was strict. Would you have the sea reclaim our walls because eight dead officers kept their trinkets?"

"They were not trinkets," Agnes said. "They were the anchors of their souls. You cast them into the inner lip to satisfy a mortgage."

The silence that followed was heavier than the stone ceiling. Malachi looked at the sheared caliper, then at Agnes. The pious facade had vanished, leaving only the cold calculation of a man who weighed salvation against solvency.

"The bell tolls for the abbey's survival," Malachi said. "The sailors are already drowned. What does it matter where their silver rests?"

Agnes looked toward the belfry. The tallow-felt muffling would hold for now, but the flood tide was rising, and the silver in the bronze was a debt the sea always collected.

The North Scriptorium smelled of kelp smoke and the sour tang of damp vellum. Outside, the gale hammered the sea-wall, a rhythmic percussion that mirrored the ticking of the Compline hour. Prior Malachi did not look up from his charcoal pan; he continued to warm his ink-horn, the orange glow casting long, flickering shadows across the vaulted stone.

Jude laid the crushed brass caliper across the Prior's clean vellum sheet. The metal was sheared, a jagged testament to the force required to jam the bell’s yoke. Jude wrapped his pinched thumb in a strip of linen, his jaw tight.

"The bell is muffled, Father Prior," Jude said. "But the metal is wrong. It’s too soft. The pour didn't set true to the bronze."

Malachi shifted his weight, his voice sliding into a practiced, clerical cadence. "The casting is a matter of artisanal variance, Jude. We are grateful the bell stands at all given the storm."

Agnes stepped forward, the soaked burial roll open upon the lectern. She did not raise her voice; she spoke with the precision of a rubric. "The Halcyon brought forty souls to our shore, Father. I have the register here. Forty names entered into the book of the dead."

Malachi finally looked at her, his eyes narrow. "A tragedy of the tide, Sister. All were given the dignity of the garth."

"Thirty-two," Agnes replied. "Only thirty-two silver neck-tallies were recovered and interred with the bodies. The register is clear. Eight tallies—the silver of the officers—are absent from the burial record."

Jude stepped closer, his voice blunt with craftsman’s anger. "Silver in a bronze pour lowers the melting point. It changes the ring. I felt it in the metal, and I see it in the slag. You didn't cast a memorial, you cast a vault."

Malachi’s composure wavered. He looked from the sheared caliper to the burial roll, the silence of the room filling with the scent of burning tallow. 

"The abbey’s dike-loan is a heavy burden," Malachi said, the evasiveness finally dropping. "The bailiff required an assay of value to secure the mortgage against the flood. The officers' silver was a windfall from the sea. To bury it in the salt-mud would have been a dereliction of my duty to this house."

"And what of the duty to the departed, Father?" Agnes asked. "The rubric demands the tally remain with the bone."

"The walls protect the living," Malachi replied.

Agnes looked toward the belfry. The bell remained silent, muffled by tallow-felt, but the knowledge of the silver remained. According to the laws of the tide, bronze cast with the rings of the drowned would toll with a hunger that no felt could stifle, unless the debt was paid in more than coin.

rounds.candidate_text:
The North Scriptorium smelled of kelp smoke and the sour tang of damp vellum. Outside, the gale hammered the sea-wall, a rhythmic percussion that mirrored the ticking of the Compline hour. Prior Malachi did not look up from his charcoal pan; he continued to warm his ink-horn, the orange glow casting long, flickering shadows across the vaulted stone.

Jude laid the crushed brass caliper across the Prior's clean vellum sheet. The metal was sheared, a jagged testament to the force required to jam the bell’s yoke. Jude wrapped his pinched thumb in a strip of linen, his jaw tight.

"The bell is muffled, Father Prior," Jude said. "But the metal is wrong. It’s too soft. The pour didn't set true to the bronze."

Malachi shifted his weight, his voice sliding into a practiced, clerical cadence. "The casting is a matter of artisanal variance, Jude. We are grateful the bell stands at all given the storm."

Agnes stepped forward, the soaked burial roll open upon the lectern. She did not raise her voice; she spoke with the precision of a rubric. "The Halcyon brought forty souls to our shore, Father. I have the register here. Forty names entered into the book of the dead."

Malachi finally looked at her, his eyes narrow. "A tragedy of the tide, Sister. All were given the dignity of the garth."

"Thirty-two," Agnes replied. "Only thirty-two silver neck-tallies were recovered and interred with the bodies. The register is clear. Eight tallies—the silver of the officers—are absent from the burial record."

Jude stepped closer, his voice blunt with craftsman’s anger. "Silver in a bronze pour lowers the melting point. It changes the ring. I felt it in the metal, and I see it in the slag. You didn't cast a memorial, you cast a vault."

Malachi’s composure wavered. He looked from the sheared caliper to the burial roll, the silence of the room filling with the scent of burning tallow. 

"The abbey’s dike-loan is a heavy burden," Malachi said, the evasiveness finally dropping. "The bailiff required an assay of value to secure the mortgage against the flood. The officers' silver was a windfall from the sea. To bury it in the salt-mud would have been a dereliction of my duty to this house."

"And what of the duty to the departed, Father?" Agnes asked. "The rubric demands the tally remain with the bone."

"The walls protect the living," Malachi replied.

Agnes looked toward the belfry. The bell remained silent, muffled by tallow-felt, but the knowledge of the silver remained. According to the laws of the tide, bronze cast with the rings of the drowned would toll with a hunger that no felt could stifle, unless the debt was paid in more than coin.

pairs.name: Keeping vigil by the salt-line on the nave flags

pov.voice_profile: Controlled, vigil-focused; measures fear through candle-inch marks, damp salt lines, and liturgy.

rounds.candidate_text:
Agnes knelt on the rush mat, her knees pressing into the damp weave. The nave was a cavern of salt-scented dark, lit only by the single hour-candle pinned to the wall. She watched the flame flicker, measuring the remaining wax against the notched marks on the tallow-stick. Six hours remained until the morning flood.

Under the heavy oak sea-doors, the limestone flags wept. Brine seeped through the joints in slow, rhythmic pulses, leaving a shimmering glaze that smelled of old depths and decayed kelp. Agnes reached for the block of fuller’s chalk. She leaned forward, her breath frosting in the chill, and drew a sharp, white line across the threshold. 

The salt had crept two flagstones further up the nave than the previous spring tide.

She stared at the line. The encroachment was a physical ledger, a record of the abbey’s slow surrender to the coast. If the water reached the third flagstone, the lower crypts would breathe the tide.

Setting the chalk aside, Agnes pulled the muffler from her lap. The tallow-felt wrap was heavy, saturated with rendered fat to repel the brine, but a jagged tear ran along the seam. She threaded her needle with waxed linen, the movement precise and practiced. 

The muffler was the only barrier against the bronze cast. Without the felt to dampen the resonance of the flood, the tide would bring the silver rings of the drowned—small, cold circles of metal that clung to the bronze like leeches, humming with a frequency that could shatter a sister's composure. To leave the muffler torn was to invite the noise of the dead into the sanctuary.

She pushed the needle through the thick, greasy felt. The fabric resisted, then gave way with a dull pop. She stitched in tight, overlapping crosses, her focus narrowing to the point of the needle and the rhythm of her own breathing. With every pull of the thread, she recited the third psalm of the vigil, binding the gap as if sealing a tomb.

A sudden draft swept through the nave, smelling of open ocean and cold iron. The candle flame flattened, nearly extinguishing. Agnes froze, her needle poised mid-air. In the sudden silence, the oak doors groaned under a pressure that should not have existed during an ebb tide. 

She looked down at the chalk line. A thin, translucent film of water was already beginning to lap over the white mark, erasing the boundary she had just drawn. The tide was returning early.

rounds.candidate_text:
Agnes knelt on the rush mat, her knees pressing into the damp weave. The nave was a cavern of cold limestone and salt-heavy air. To her left, the hour-candle burned in its iron bracket, the wax dripping in slow, rhythmic beads that marked the passage of the ebb tide. Six hours remained before the flood returned to claim the threshold.

She reached for the block of fuller’s chalk. The limestone flags beneath her were weeping, a thin sheen of brine seeping through the gaps in the masonry under the oak sea-doors. Agnes leaned forward, the chalk scratching a stark white line across the gray stone. She traced the furthest reach of the previous tide, noting the seepage. Each spring tide crept two flagstones further up the nave, claiming the sanctuary inch by inch.

Once the line was drawn, she set the chalk aside and pulled the muffler into her lap. The tallow-felt wrap was heavy, smelling of rendered fat and old seawater. It had been torn during the last surge, a jagged rent along the seam where the pressure of the tide had forced it against the bronze casting. 

She threaded the heavy needle with waxed linen. The work required a disciplined hand. If the muffler failed, the bronze would be left exposed to the flood, and the tide would cast back the silver rings of the drowned men—small, cold tokens of a debt the Abbey could not afford to acknowledge.

The needle pierced the thick felt with a dull pop. Agnes stitched in a tight overcast pattern, pulling the linen taut to seal the gap. She focused on the tactile resistance of the fabric, the way the tallow left a greasy residue on her fingertips. The silence of the nave was absolute, save for the distant, rhythmic drip of condensation from the vaulted ceiling.

She paused, glancing toward the west doors. The oak groaned under the external pressure of the receding sea, a low, guttural sound that vibrated through the floor. She checked the candle. Two inches of wax remained.

Agnes tied off the final knot and smoothed the felt. The repair was secure. She stood slowly, her joints stiff from the cold, and looked at the white chalk line. The brine was already beginning to blur the edges of the mark, the stone drinking the salt. She gathered her tools, the weight of the mended muffler in her arms a necessary shield against the coming flood.

pairs.name: Keeping vigil by the salt-line on the nave flags

pov.voice_profile: Controlled, vigil-focused; measures fear through candle-inch marks, damp salt lines, and liturgy.

rounds.candidate_text:
Agnes knelt on the rush mat, the limestone flags beneath her damp with a brine that never truly dried. The air in the nave tasted of old salt and cold iron. To her left, the hour-candle burned in its brass socket, the wax dripping in slow, rhythmic beads that marked the ebb tide. Six hours remained before the flood returned to press against the oak sea-doors.

She reached for the block of fuller’s chalk. With a steady hand, she traced a white line across the threshold, marking the furthest reach of the last seepage. The salt had crept two flagstones further up the nave since the previous spring tide. Agnes noted the distance with a precise, internal tally. The sea was claiming the sanctuary inch by inch, a slow migration of water that now reached the base of the first choir pillar.

Setting the chalk aside, she unfolded the tallow-felt muffler. The heavy fabric was stiff, saturated with rendered fat to repel the tide, but a jagged tear ran along the seam. If the felt failed, the bronze cast of the west door would be exposed. Without the muffler, the flood tide would bring the silver rings of the drowned, those metallic offerings that clung to the bronze like parasites, dragging the weight of the deep into the house of God.

Agnes threaded her needle. The tallow made the felt slippery, resisting the puncture of the steel. She pushed the needle through the thick weave, her movements disciplined and slow. Each stitch was a prayer of containment. She pulled the waxed thread tight, closing the gap in the fabric to ensure the seal remained absolute.

A sudden draft swept through the nave, extinguishing the candle. The darkness was immediate and heavy, smelling of wet stone and deep-water rot. Agnes did not move. She remained still on her mat, listening to the silence of the abbey. From the loft above, the echo of Jude’s hammer had long since ceased, leaving only the sound of the distant, rhythmic thrum of the tide pulling away from the shore.

She felt the cold seep through her habit, a reminder that the limestone was porous. The water was not merely outside the doors; it lived within the stone, waiting for the moon to pull it back. Agnes reached out in the dark, her fingers finding the rough texture of the mended felt. She smoothed the fabric over the bronze, ensuring no gap remained for the silver rings to find. The vigil was a matter of millimeters, and the cost of a loose stitch was a sanctuary filled with the dead.

pairs.name: Chiseling the eighth name inside the sound-bow

pov.voice_profile: Foundryman's eye for mold-seams, wax letters, and metal grain.

rounds.candidate_text:
The timber platform groaned under my weight, wedged tight against the twelve-hundredweight bronze. I lay on my back, shoulders pressed into the rough-hewn beams, staring up into the hollow of the bell's lip. Above me, Sister Agnes held the beeswax taper. The flame flickered in the salt-damp air, casting a yellow, trembling light across the interior rim.

Seven white silver blisters had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those were the Halcyon men, their rings cast upside down in the cope to hide the theft. The metal had accepted them greedily, fusing the silver into the bronze.

I shifted my grip on the cold cape-chisel, my muscles aching from the cramped angle. There was one tally left.

"The tide is slack," Agnes said. Her voice was a thin wire in the silence of the belfry. "Ninety minutes until the flood."

I didn't answer. I focused on the eighth mark, a stubborn knot of verdigris and slag clinging to the bronze. This one felt different. The grain of the metal around it was tighter, the casting seam slightly offset. I knew how a founder worked; if you wanted to hide a name, you pressed the wax letters deep into the false-bell before ramming the cope, ensuring the silver would be swallowed by the pour.

I set the blade against the edge of the silver blister and tapped. A flake of green corrosion chipped away. I tapped again, scraping the slag with a steady, rhythmic precision. The silver began to emerge, not with the anchor of the northern fleet, but with a different crest—a stylized wave and a broken mast.

I scraped one last time, clearing the center of the stamp.

"This isn't from the Halcyon," I said, my voice hushed.

Agnes leaned in, the taper illuminating the small, polished surface. I pointed to the letters etched into the silver.

*Martin Vale.*

The silence that followed was heavier than the bell. Agnes froze, the flame of the taper dancing near the bronze. She stared at the name, her eyes tracing the letters over and over, her breathing shallow.

"Vale," she whispered. She paused, the realization clicking into place. "The Prior's brother."

I looked at the silver, then at the massive wall of the belfry. The Prior had claimed the sea-wall was funded by a pious bequest, a miracle of providence that saved the abbey from the encroaching tide. Now I saw the truth of the foundation. The Halcyon men were opportunistic additions, but Martin Vale had been the anchor. The insurance from the Anne-Marie wreck ten years ago hadn't gone to a widow or a parish; it had bought the stone that kept the Prior's feet dry.

The bell hummed faintly, a low vibration that felt like a warning. We were out of time. The flood tide was turning, and the drowned were still calling from the metal.

rounds.candidate_text:
The timber platform groaned under my weight, wedged tight against the twelve-hundredweight bronze. I lay on my back, shoulders pressed into the rough-hewn beams, staring up into the hollow of the bell's lip. Above me, Sister Agnes held the beeswax taper. The flame flickered in the salt-damp air, casting a yellow, trembling light across the interior rim.

Seven white silver blisters had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those were the Halcyon men, their rings cast upside down in the cope to hide the theft. The metal had accepted them greedily, fusing the silver into the bronze.

I shifted my grip on the cold cape-chisel, my muscles aching from the cramped angle. There was one tally left.

"The tide is slack," Agnes said. Her voice was a thin wire in the silence of the belfry. "Ninety minutes until the flood."

I didn't answer. I focused on the eighth mark, a stubborn knot of verdigris and slag clinging to the bronze. This one felt different. The grain of the metal around it was tighter, the casting seam slightly offset. I knew how a founder worked; if you wanted to hide a name, you pressed the wax letters deep into the false-bell before ramming the cope, ensuring the silver would be swallowed by the pour.

I set the blade against the edge of the silver blister and tapped. A flake of green corrosion chipped away. I tapped again, scraping the slag with a steady, rhythmic precision. The silver began to emerge, not with the anchor of the northern fleet, but with a different crest—a stylized wave and a broken mast.

I scraped one last time, clearing the center of the stamp.

"This isn't from the Halcyon," I said, my voice hushed.

Agnes leaned in, the taper illuminating the small, polished surface. I pointed to the letters etched into the silver.

*Martin Vale.*

The silence that followed was heavier than the bell. Agnes froze, the flame of the taper dancing near the bronze. She stared at the name, her eyes tracing the letters over and over, her breathing shallow.

"Vale," she whispered. She paused, the realization clicking into place. "The Prior's brother."

I looked at the silver, then at the massive wall of the belfry. The Prior had claimed the sea-wall was funded by a pious bequest, a miracle of providence that saved the abbey from the encroaching tide. Now I saw the truth of the foundation. The Halcyon men were opportunistic additions, but Martin Vale had been the anchor. The insurance from the Anne-Marie wreck ten years ago hadn't gone to a widow or a parish; it had bought the stone that kept the Prior's feet dry.

The bell hummed faintly, a low vibration that felt like a warning. We were out of time. The flood tide was turning, and the drowned were still calling from the metal.

The timber platform groaned under my weight, the wood damp with the salt-mist that always seeped through the belfry slats. I was wedged shoulders-deep beneath the bronze lip of the great bell, my neck strained against the cold metal. Above me, twelve hundredweight of bronze hung like a suspended mountain, waiting for the tide to turn.

Agnes stood inside the bell's mouth, her silhouette a thin shadow against the grey pre-dawn light. She held the beeswax taper steady, the flame licking the interior curve of the rim. The light cast a harsh, yellow glare on the eighth silver blister. It was buried deeper than the others, choked by a thick crust of verdigris and slag.

Seven white silver tallies had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those had been easy—the *Halcyon* officers, cast upside down in the cope to hide their theft. But this last one resisted.

I set the edge of the cold cape-chisel against the rim. I knew how the founder had worked this; he had pressed the wax letters into the false-bell before the cope was rammed, sealing the silver rings into the bronze grain. If the metal had cooled too quickly, the silver would have bonded to the copper, making it a part of the bell's very soul.

"Steady," I whispered.

I struck the chisel with a sharp, measured blow. A flake of green oxide chipped away. I struck again, scraping the slag from the silver face. The metal didn't pop free like the others. It was anchored.

As the last of the crust fell, the taper's light hit the engraving. I stopped. The stamp wasn't an anchor. There was no fleet mark here. Instead, the silver bore a name in a tight, archaic script: *Martin Vale*.

I slid out from under the lip, my muscles cramping. I didn't look at Agnes; I looked at the name.

"The *Halcyon* went down three years ago," I said, my voice sounding hollow in the belfry. "Martin Vale died ten years ago on the *Anne-Marie*."

Agnes leaned over, her eyes narrowing as she read the silver. She went very still. "Vale," she murmured. "That was the Prior's name. Before the vows."

The realization settled in the cold air between us. The Prior hadn't just scavenged the silver of strangers to build the abbey's sea-wall. He had fused his own brother's ring into the bronze, and I felt a sudden, visceral shudder at the thought of that silver vein running through the metal I had just touched.

A distant swell hit the cliffs below. The slack water was ending. In ninety minutes, the flood tide would return, and unless we muffled this bell in tallow-felt, the drowned would ring their claim.

rounds.candidate_text:
The timber platform groaned under my weight, the wood damp with the salt-mist that always seeped through the belfry slats. I was wedged shoulders-deep beneath the bronze lip of the great bell, my neck strained against the cold metal. Above me, twelve hundredweight of bronze hung like a suspended mountain, waiting for the tide to turn.

Agnes stood inside the bell's mouth, her silhouette a thin shadow against the grey pre-dawn light. She held the beeswax taper steady, the flame licking the interior curve of the rim. The light cast a harsh, yellow glare on the eighth silver blister. It was buried deeper than the others, choked by a thick crust of verdigris and slag.

Seven white silver tallies had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those had been easy—the *Halcyon* officers, cast upside down in the cope to hide their theft. But this last one resisted.

I set the edge of the cold cape-chisel against the rim. I knew how the founder had worked this; he had pressed the wax letters into the false-bell before the cope was rammed, sealing the silver rings into the bronze grain. If the metal had cooled too quickly, the silver would have bonded to the copper, making it a part of the bell's very soul.

"Steady," I whispered.

I struck the chisel with a sharp, measured blow. A flake of green oxide chipped away. I struck again, scraping the slag from the silver face. The metal didn't pop free like the others. It was anchored.

As the last of the crust fell, the taper's light hit the engraving. I stopped. The stamp wasn't an anchor. There was no fleet mark here. Instead, the silver bore a name in a tight, archaic script: *Martin Vale*.

I slid out from under the lip, my muscles cramping. I didn't look at Agnes; I looked at the name.

"The *Halcyon* went down three years ago," I said, my voice sounding hollow in the belfry. "Martin Vale died ten years ago on the *Anne-Marie*."

Agnes leaned over, her eyes narrowing as she read the silver. She went very still. "Vale," she murmured. "That was the Prior's name. Before the vows."

The realization settled in the cold air between us. The Prior hadn't just scavenged the silver of strangers to build the abbey's sea-wall. He had fused his own brother's ring into the bronze, and I felt a sudden, visceral shudder at the thought of that silver vein running through the metal I had just touched.

A distant swell hit the cliffs below. The slack water was ending. In ninety minutes, the flood tide would return, and unless we muffled this bell in tallow-felt, the drowned would ring their claim.

rounds.candidate_text:
The bronze lip of the bell pressed into my shoulder, cold and smelling of old salt. I was wedged tight against the timber platform, my breath frosting in the pre-dawn air. Beside me, Sister Agnes held the beeswax taper steady. The flame flickered, casting long, dancing shadows across the interior curve of the twelve-hundredweight casting.

Seven white silver blisters had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those were the Halcyon men, their rings cast upside down in the cope to bind them to the metal. I had cleared the slag from the seventh, but the eighth tally remained, buried deeper in the rim.

I shifted my weight, feeling the grit of the belfry floor beneath my boots. Low slack water. The tide was holding its breath, but I knew the clock. In ninety minutes, the morning flood would surge into the tower, and if these silver anchors were still embedded in the bronze, the bell would ring with the voices of the drowned.

"There," Agnes whispered.

I saw it. A stubborn knot of verdigris and oxidized lead, masking the final stamp. I set the edge of the cold chisel against the metal, feeling for the seam where the wax letter had once been pressed into the false-bell before the cope was rammed. I struck the handle with a sharp, controlled blow.

A flake of green crust snapped away. I scraped again, slower this time, peeling back the corrosion to reveal the silver beneath.

The stamp was different. There was no northern fleet anchor here. Instead, the silver bore a crisp, deep-set engraving of a merchant’s scale and a name.

I wiped the metal clean with a rag.

"It isn't a Halcyon officer," I said, my voice hushed in the hollow of the bell.

Agnes leaned in, the taper illuminating the inscription. The flame wavered violently as her hand jerked.

"Martin Vale," she read.

The name hung between us. I knew the history of the abbey’s sea-wall—the massive granite barrier that kept the Atlantic from swallowing the nave. It had been funded by a sudden, immense insurance windfall a decade ago, a payout from the wreck of the Anne-Marie.

"The Prior's brother," Agnes said.

I looked up at the bronze ceiling. The Prior had not just stolen the silver of strangers to fortify his abbey; he had anchored his own blood to the bell to ensure the wall stood. The debt wasn't opportunistic. It was a family pact cast in metal.

The wind shifted, bringing the scent of brine and rising water. The tide was turning.

rounds.candidate_text:
The bronze lip of the bell pressed into my shoulder, cold and smelling of old salt. I was wedged tight against the timber platform, my breath frosting in the pre-dawn air. Beside me, Sister Agnes held the beeswax taper steady. The flame flickered, casting long, dancing shadows across the interior curve of the twelve-hundredweight casting.

Seven white silver blisters had already come away under my chisel, each stamped with the anchor of the northern fleet. Those were the Halcyon men, their rings cast upside down in the cope to bind them to the metal. I had cleared the slag from the seventh, but the eighth tally remained, buried deeper in the rim.

I shifted my weight, feeling the grit of the belfry floor beneath my boots. Low slack water. The tide was holding its breath, but I knew the clock. In ninety minutes, the morning flood would surge into the tower, and if these silver anchors were still embedded in the bronze, the bell would ring with the voices of the drowned.

"There," Agnes whispered.

I saw it. A stubborn knot of verdigris and oxidized lead, masking the final stamp. I set the edge of the cold chisel against the metal, feeling for the seam where the wax letter had once been pressed into the false-bell before the cope was rammed. I struck the handle with a sharp, controlled blow.

A flake of green crust snapped away. I scraped again, slower this time, peeling back the corrosion to reveal the silver beneath.

The stamp was different. There was no northern fleet anchor here. Instead, the silver bore a crisp, deep-set engraving of a merchant’s scale and a name.

I wiped the metal clean with a rag.

"It isn't a Halcyon officer," I said, my voice hushed in the hollow of the bell.

Agnes leaned in, the taper illuminating the inscription. The flame wavered violently as her hand jerked.

"Martin Vale," she read.

The name hung between us. I knew the history of the abbey’s sea-wall—the massive granite barrier that kept the Atlantic from swallowing the nave. It had been funded by a sudden, immense insurance windfall a decade ago, a payout from the wreck of the Anne-Marie.

"The Prior's brother," Agnes said.

I looked up at the bronze ceiling. The Prior had not just stolen the silver of strangers to fortify his abbey; he had anchored his own blood to the bell to ensure the wall stood. The debt wasn't opportunistic. It was a family pact cast in metal.

The wind shifted, bringing the scent of brine and rising water. The tide was turning.

rounds.candidate_text:
The last sod of salt-turf settled over the seven Halcyon curls in the garth. Agnes stepped away from the consecrated earth, her palms raw and stained with lime. Beside her, Jude was already packing his chisels into a heavy canvas roll, the metal clinking with a finality that matched the graying light of the horizon.

They walked in silence toward the Low Causeway. The air tasted of brine and old iron. As they descended the slope toward the tide-line, the Leper’s Cross emerged from the mist, its barnacle-crusted stone leaning away from the wind. Below them, the sea was a slate-colored heave, the flood-turn beginning its slow, inevitable push inward.

Agnes reached into her habit and withdrew the eighth silver shaving. Martin Vale’s tally was a jagged sliver, cold against her skin. She looked up at the abbey tower. The bell hung muffled in tallow-felt, a dead weight of bronze that should have screamed as the tide reclaimed the shore. 

"The notches are deep," Jude said, his voice low. "It will ring flat by a quarter-tone now. Forever."

Agnes did not answer. She stepped to the edge of the causeway, where the first tongue of the incoming tide licked the base of the cross. She opened her hand. The silver curl fell, a momentary spark against the gray, and vanished into the churning foam of the channel.

The water surged. The flood-tide hit the causeway with a heavy, rhythmic thrum, but the bell remained silent. No spectral chime rose to meet the water; the drowned names were returned, the supernatural debt settled by the stricture of the salt and the soil.

Agnes watched the foam recede from the stone, her raw palms stinging in the salt air. The bell was a dead thing now, stripped of its voices.

A rhythmic drumming sounded from the distance—hooves on the stone of the low causeway. Through the thinning mist, a rider appeared, his cloak snapping in the wind. It was the dike-reeve’s bailiff, his face set in a mask of bureaucratic patience. He stopped his horse ten paces from them, the animal shifting its weight in the shallow wash.

"Sister Agnes," the bailiff called, his voice cutting through the salt wind. "The equinox has passed. The lease on the northern dike is three days overdue, and the Reeve does not accept prayers in lieu of silver."

Agnes looked at her empty palms, then back at the silent tower. The bell was quiet, but the abbey was bankrupt.

The last sod of salt-turf settled over the seven Halcyon curls in the garth. Agnes stepped away from the consecrated earth, her palms raw and stained with lime. Beside her, Jude was already packing his chisels into a heavy canvas roll, the metal clinking with a finality that matched the graying light of the horizon.

They walked in silence toward the Low Causeway. The air tasted of brine and old iron. As they descended the slope toward the tide-line, the Leper’s Cross emerged from the mist, its barnacle-crusted stone leaning away from the wind. Below them, the sea was a slate-colored heave, the flood-turn beginning its slow, inevitable push inward.

Agnes reached into her habit and withdrew the eighth silver shaving. Martin Vale’s tally was a jagged sliver, cold against her skin. She looked up at the abbey tower. The bell hung muffled in tallow-felt, a dead weight of bronze that should have screamed as the tide reclaimed the shore. 

"The notches are deep," Jude said, his voice low. "It will ring flat by a quarter-tone now. Forever."

Agnes did not answer. She stepped to the edge of the causeway, where the first tongue of the incoming tide licked the base of the cross. She opened her hand. The silver curl fell, a momentary spark against the gray, and vanished into the churning foam of the channel.

The water surged. The flood-tide hit the causeway with a heavy, rhythmic thrum, but the bell remained silent. No spectral chime rose to meet the water; the drowned names were returned, the supernatural debt settled by the stricture of the salt and the soil.

Agnes watched the foam recede from the stone, her raw palms stinging in the salt air. The bell was a dead thing now, stripped of its voices.

A rhythmic drumming sounded from the distance—hooves on the stone of the low causeway. Through the thinning mist, a rider appeared, his cloak snapping in the wind. It was the dike-reeve’s bailiff, his face set in a mask of bureaucratic patience. He stopped his horse ten paces from them, the animal shifting its weight in the shallow wash.

"Sister Agnes," the bailiff called, his voice cutting through the salt wind. "The equinox has passed. The lease on the northern dike is three days overdue, and the Reeve does not accept prayers in lieu of silver."

Agnes looked at her empty palms, then back at the silent tower. The bell was quiet, but the abbey was bankrupt.

The last sod of salt-turf settled over the seven Halcyon curls in the garth. Agnes stepped away from the consecrated earth, her fingers raw and stained with lime. He did not speak; he only watched the horizon where the sea began its inward push.

They walked in silence toward the Low Causeway. The tide was turning, the water creeping back toward the abbey walls in a slow, rhythmic surge. At the tide-line stood the Leper’s Cross, a barnacle-crusted pillar of stone that marked the boundary between the living and the lost.

Agnes reached into her habit and withdrew the eighth silver shaving. This curl belonged to Martin Vale. While the others had been returned to the earth, the eighth required the channel.

She stepped onto the slick stones of the causeway. The water swirled around her ankles, cold enough to numb the skin. She held the silver tally aloft for a moment, the metal dull under the colorless sky. With a sharp flick of her wrist, she cast the shaving into the churning foam. It vanished instantly, swallowed by the flood-turn.

Above them, the mourning-bell hung in its tower, muffled with tallow-felt. As the tide reached its peak, the moment arrived when the drowned names usually demanded their toll. Agnes waited, her breath shallow. The wind whipped her veil against her cheek. The bell remained silent. The debt of the drowned was paid; the silver was gone, and Agnes knew that when the tallow-felt was finally stripped, the bell would ring flat by a quarter-tone.

Jude let out a long, slow breath. "It is quiet," he said.

"The dead are satisfied," Agnes replied.

He did not stop to greet them. He pulled the horse to a halt ten paces away, his face hard and official.

"Sister Agnes," the bailiff called, his voice cutting through the salt wind. "The equinox has passed. The abbey’s lease on the northern dike is three days overdue. The reeve will not accept prayers in lieu of silver this season."

Agnes looked at her empty hands, then back at the silent bell tower. The supernatural terror had been averted, but the secular world arrived with the sun. The abbey was solvent in the eyes of the ghosts, but bankrupt in the eyes of the law.

The relief was brief. As the first sliver of gold broke the horizon, a rhythmic thud echoed from the distance. Agnes turned. A rider was approaching on the low causeway, his horse splashing through the receding shallows. The man wore the heavy wool and polished leather of the dike-reeve’s bailiff.

He did not stop to greet them. He pulled the horse to a halt ten paces away, his face hard and official.

"Sister Agnes," the bailiff called, his voice cutting through the salt wind. "The equinox has passed. The abbey’s lease on the northern dike is three days overdue. The reeve will not accept prayers in lieu of silver this season."

Agnes looked at her empty hands, then back at the silent bell tower. The supernatural terror had been averted, but the secular world arrived with the sun. The abbey was solvent in the eyes of the ghosts, but bankrupt in the eyes of the law.
